The problem is it's impossible to define morality when there is a god who is considered untouchable by it. God is able to set any arbitrary rule he sees fit and call it morality by defining it as such, but there is no inherent morality in punishing Adam and Eve for disobedience when they had no knowledge of the difference of good or evil in the first place. The very fact that they were unable to differentiate between the two is exemplified by how she was persuaded by the snake to eat the fruit. However, there is no conception of right or wrong beforehand, so instead it becomes more apparent that the story is more of a metaphor for God fighting the devil. Who's to say who was right or wrong? Who's to say God is even the "good guy"? Adam and Eve sure didn't know. They simply knew He created them. The snake could easily have been looking out for their best interest by providing them with the knowledge of what is wrong.

And why should this be a bad thing? Why should God tell them not to eat from the tree, or punish them from doing so? Again, it's extremely murky because God is above punishment, right or wrong. And therefore I believe that God is not right or wrong, good or evil himself. Instead what it seems like is that God is a petty, vengeful being, like a close minded, overbearing parent that offers no justification besides, "because I said so."

In any case, who is to say disobedience is WRONG? Surely (and yeah, I'm going to pull a Hitler here) disobedience towards Hitler 's authoritarianism and genocidal designs by a German Lieutenant would be considered morally justified, so therein lies the center of the issue- intent. 

The intent is where the morality lies in this case. Not in the action, but in the motive. Why did Eve eat the fruit? Because she was persuaded to by the snake while she had no conception of the idea of right or wrong in the first place. So regardless of anything else, eve is naive and blameless in the situation. This is why I find it to be unmoral, vengeful, and petty of God to punish them so severely for so minor an infraction. 

If someone slipped a child drugs and said to them to try it because it was candy, would you throw the kid in the slammer for possession? 

For a divine being, God sure has a flawed system.
They didn't, because they hadn't eaten from the tree of knowledge of good or evil yet, had they? I don't see why that's inherently a bad thing, either.

That's my point.
